metadata.title: The Same Math Twice
metadata.purpose: Provenance Gatekeeper Development Log, Week 11 — putting a Redis layer in front of the embedding and vector-search path, what the measured speed-up actually is, and the cost of caching a verdict in a system whose job is to be right.

metadata.series_note: No prior reel covers caching — checked across all 20 built reels. Phase 2 of the architecture opens here. The added beat is specific to THIS system: caching a verification verdict is different from caching a search result, because the thing being cached is a judgement about whether something is true.

beats.narration_text: Hi, I am Onkar Bhujbal. The Provenance Gatekeeper is secure and it is automated. It is also slow. Turning a claim into an embedding and searching the vector store is real compute, and if the model produces the same financial claim ten times, I pay for that math ten times. Nothing about the tenth one is new. This week starts Phase 2: a Redis layer in front of the expensive path.

beats.narration_text: The cache is the easy part. Deciding how long the Gatekeeper is allowed to repeat an old verdict is the part that needed thinking about — because a stale verdict is not a slow answer, it is a wrong one.

beats.authoring_note: Both readings are true sentences: 'Caching answers is easy.' and, corrected, 'Caching verdicts is easy.' — the swap moves the beat onto what is actually being stored.

beats.narration_text: The Docker Compose file now brings up an Alpine Redis container alongside the A.P.I. and the vector store, on the same internal network we set up a few weeks ago — so it is not reachable from outside the stack. Redis sits between FastAPI and ChromaDB. A repeat claim is intercepted there and never reaches the embedding model at all.

stages.name: CHROMADB

beats.authoring_note: The internal-network point is carried over from the Week 9 reel's Docker beat, where it was established — a new container on a stack is a new thing to not expose.

beats.narration_text: The logic is about as simple as code gets. A claim arrives, the Gatekeeper builds a key and asks Redis. If the answer is there — a cache hit — it returns immediately. If it is not, it falls through to ChromaDB, does the heavy work, and writes the result back with a one-hour expiry. Note what is in that key, because the next two minutes of this video are about what happens when something is missing from it.

props.title: verify_claim()
props.code:
key = f"verdict:{corpus_version}:{sha256(claim)}"

if (hit := redis_client.get(key)) is not None:
    return json.loads(hit)          # cache HIT

verdict = run_vector_verification(claim)   # MISS

redis_client.setex(key, 3600, json.dumps(verdict))
return verdict

# The key is the contract.
# Anything it omits, you are promising
# does not change the answer.
props.sparkLine: A hit returns before the model wakes up.

beats.honesty_note: Reconstructed from the logic described in the script (redis_client.get / setex, one-hour expiry). The corpus_version component in the key is the reel's addition and is argued for in B05.

beats.narration_text: The numbers are good, and I want to be exact about what they are. Running locally, a cold verification — embedding plus vector search — took roughly four hundred and fifty milliseconds. On a cache hit, the same claim came back in under fifteen. That is a real improvement on the read path. What it is not is a scale test. It is one machine, a warm cache, and no concurrency, so it tells us the hit is cheap. It does not tell us what happens at a thousand requests a second.

beats.honesty_note: SCOPED. The script says the gains are 'staggering' and that this allows the Gatekeeper 'to handle massive enterprise scale.' The ~450ms and <15ms figures are Onkar's own local measurements and are reported as such; the enterprise-scale conclusion does not follow from a warm single-request timing and has been removed. The component breakdown (120/300/30) is an illustrative split of his stated ~450ms total, not separately measured.

beats.narration_text: So here is what worries me about this change. Everywhere else, a stale cache entry costs you an out-of-date number. Here, the thing I am caching is a verdict — a judgement about whether a claim is true. If someone corrects the source ledger at nine fifteen, the Gatekeeper keeps returning the verdict it computed against the old ledger until the hour runs out. It will block a claim that is now correct, or pass one that is now wrong, and it will do it with full confidence. That is why the corpus version belongs in the key: when the ledger changes, every verdict computed against the old one should stop existing.

beats.authoring_note: BEAT ADDED, and it is why the reel exists. The script treats the cache purely as a speed win. For a hallucination-interception service the cached object is a VERDICT, so a stale entry is not a slow answer — it is a wrong verification, in both directions. The corpus_version key component shown in B03 is the fix this beat argues for.

beats.narration_text: So: compute is expensive and R.A.M. is cheap by comparison — cache your results and save the processors for novel problems. But if what you are caching is a decision rather than a number, version the key against the evidence, and drop the whole generation when the evidence moves.

props.title: ingest.py — on ledger change
props.code:
def on_ledger_write(rows):
    write_to_chroma(rows)
    bump("corpus_version")   # verdicts keyed on it
                             # are now unreachable

# TASK: don't do the same math twice.

# Cache a number -> it goes stale.
# Cache a verdict -> it goes WRONG.
# Version the key against the evidence.
props.sparkLine: Expire the evidence, not the clock.

beats.honesty_note: This is the recommended shape, not a listing of shipped code — `ingest.py` has still never been supplied to this project, and the reel does not pretend otherwise.

beats.narration_text: Here is the prompt worth running against your own cache. Ask a model what the longest possible gap is between your source of truth changing and your users seeing the new answer — and whether anything in your system would tell you that gap had been exceeded. For most caches the honest answer to the second half is no.

beats.narration_text: Don't do the same math twice — and don't let an old answer outlive the evidence it was built on. Onkar Bhujbal, for Humanitarians AI.
